claims.text: The starting material is a W–Cu composite containing tungsten particles or an interconnected tungsten ligament network embedded in a copper matrix.
The tungsten particles or ligaments will be coated with a 50–100 nm nickel layer before consolidation and joint fabrication.
A nickel coating will improve wettability at the W–Cu interface.
A nickel coating will reduce interfacial energy at the W–Cu interface.
Improved wettability and reduced interfacial energy will promote a more coherent bond between tungsten and copper.
The nickel layer will act as a diffusion barrier that suppresses phase separation.
The nickel layer will mitigate nucleation of interfacial voids.
Enhanced wetting and bonding will minimize thermodynamically driven W–Cu compositional segregation during high-temperature service.
The nickel interlayer will limit irradiation-induced defect accumulation.
Suppression of segregation, irradiation-induced defects, and interfacial voids will sustain a better thermal-conduction path across the W–Cu interface.
The nickel-coated composite will have a statistically significant increase in effective thermal conductivity relative to an identically processed uncoated composite.
The thermal-conductivity increase will result from reduced W–Cu interfacial thermal resistance.
After thermal and irradiation exposure, the nickel-coated composite will have a lower density of interfacial voids than the uncoated baseline.
The intervention is anticipated to remain beneficial at service temperatures up to approximately 1000 °C.
The intervention is anticipated to remain beneficial under moderate irradiation fluences typical of plasma-facing component joints.
The intervention may cease to be effective at temperatures significantly above 1000 °C or at ultra-high irradiation doses.
